question: According to G.B. Shaw, what is the unavoidable 'natural slavery' that every human being is subjected to from birth? 🧬
options: Working for a cruel boss 👔
Paying taxes to the government 💸
The biological need to eat, drink, and sleep 🥪
Following the laws of the country 📜
answer: The biological need to eat, drink, and sleep 🥪
explanation: Brilliant! Shaw argues that before society even imposes rules on us, nature makes us its slaves. We are forced to spend a large portion of our lives eating, sleeping, and drinking just to survive! 🌍
hint: It is something your body forces you to do, regardless of the laws.

question: How does Shaw define 'unnatural slavery' in his essay? ⛓️
options: Animals kept in a zoo 🦁
Man being forced to work for the profit of another man 🏭
Living in a very cold climate ❄️
Studying for long hours in school 📚
answer: Man being forced to work for the profit of another man 🏭
explanation: Spot on! While natural slavery is biological, 'unnatural slavery' occurs under capitalism when one human being is forced to sell their labor to enrich a master just to avoid starvation. 🎩
hint: Think about human-to-human exploitation.

question: What is the 'whip' that Nature uses to enforce its natural slavery upon us? 🌿
options: The police force 🚔
Hunger and thirst 🍽️
The legal justice system ⚖️
Social media pressure 📱
answer: Hunger and thirst 🍽️
explanation: Excellent! Nature doesn't need police to make us eat or sleep. It uses the harsh 'whips' of hunger, thirst, and exhaustion to force us into obedience. 🛌
hint: It is a physical sensation that tells you to eat.

question: Approximately how many hours a day does Shaw estimate are taken up by our 'natural slavery' (sleeping, eating, washing)? ⏰
options: 4 hours ⏳
8 hours ⌚
12 hours 🕛
20 hours 🕰️
answer: 12 hours 🕛
explanation: Fantastic! Shaw calculates that human beings spend at least half their day (about 12 hours) just maintaining their bodies through sleep, meals, and hygiene. 🚿
hint: It is exactly half of a standard 24-hour day.

question: What does Shaw consider to be 'true freedom' for a human being? 🕊️
options: Never having to eat or sleep again 🤖
Having plenty of leisure time to do exactly as one pleases 🎨
Being a famous politician 🏛️
Owning a lot of factories 🏭
answer: Having plenty of leisure time to do exactly as one pleases 🎨
explanation: Awesome! True freedom, according to Shaw, exists only in our leisure time—the hours where we are neither serving nature's biology nor a capitalist master. 🎸
hint: It relates to free time and personal choice.

question: How does Shaw view the concept of voting in a democratic election? 🗳️
options: As the ultimate proof of absolute freedom 🗽
As a sacred duty of every citizen 🦅
As an illusion where you merely choose which master will rule you 🎭
As a way to abolish natural slavery 🧬
answer: As an illusion where you merely choose which master will rule you 🎭
explanation: Brilliant! Shaw uses sharp satire to point out that voting doesn't make you free; it just gives you the illusion of freedom by letting you pick between two masters. 🎩
hint: He thinks it is a bit of a trick played on the public.

question: Who are 'Tweedledum and Tweedledee' in Shaw's essay? 👯‍♂️
options: Two famous poets ✒️
Two rival political candidates who are essentially the same 🗳️
Two factory workers 🛠️
Two ancient philosophers 📜
answer: Two rival political candidates who are essentially the same 🗳️
explanation: Spot on! Shaw borrows these characters from Alice in Wonderland to mock politicians. He argues that rival candidates are practically identical, offering no real change for the worker. 👔
hint: They are people you might vote for in an election.

question: Why does the worker accept unnatural slavery (working for a capitalist) according to Shaw? 😨
options: Because they enjoy the hard labor 🏋️
Because they want to be famous 📸
Because the alternative is starvation 🍞
Because the government physically forces them 🚔
answer: Because the alternative is starvation 🍞
explanation: Excellent! The capitalist master doesn't need to whip the worker; the fear of losing their job and starving is enough to keep them working. 🍽️
hint: Think about the basic human need for survival.

question: In Shaw's view, who owns the time of the worker during their shift? ⏳
options: The worker themselves 🙋
The capitalist master 🎩
The government 🏛️
Mother Nature 🌿
answer: The capitalist master 🎩
explanation: Fantastic! Once a worker sells their labor, those hours belong entirely to the master. During that time, the worker has absolutely zero freedom. 🏭
hint: It is the person who pays the wages.

question: Which literary device does Shaw heavily rely on when he says people sing 'Britons never shall be slaves' while actually being wage slaves? 🎭
options: Personification 🗣️
Alliteration 🔡
Irony and Satire 🃏
Simile 🪞
answer: Irony and Satire 🃏
explanation: Awesome! Shaw loves using irony and satire. He highlights the sheer paradox of people proudly singing about freedom while spending their whole lives working for a boss! 🎵
hint: It is a device used to mock a contradiction between reality and belief.

question: According to Shaw, what is the 'catch' with natural slavery? 🎣
options: It only applies to poor people 🏚️
It is an absolute necessity that applies equally to everyone, rich or poor 🌍
It can be easily avoided with money 💸
It only happens in the winter ❄️
answer: It is an absolute necessity that applies equally to everyone, rich or poor 🌍
explanation: Brilliant! Nature is a perfectly fair master. Whether you are a king or a beggar, you still have to eat, sleep, and use the bathroom. 👑
hint: Nature does not discriminate based on wealth.

question: How does Shaw describe the typical life of women in terms of slavery? 👩‍🍳
options: They are the freest people in society 🕊️
They are enslaved by domestic chores and household management 🧹
They are naturally masters over men 👑
They only experience natural slavery 🧬
answer: They are enslaved by domestic chores and household management 🧹
explanation: Spot on! Shaw acknowledges that women face a specific type of unnatural slavery: the unpaid, continuous drudgery of housekeeping and domestic chores. 🏡
hint: Think about traditional gender roles in household duties.

question: What is Shaw's perspective on the 'master class' (the wealthy capitalists)? 🎩
options: They enjoy absolute, unrestricted freedom 🦅
They are entirely evil and heartless 😈
They are also slaves to their property, anxieties, and social duties 📉
They work harder than the factory workers 🛠️
answer: They are also slaves to their property, anxieties, and social duties 📉
explanation: Excellent! Shaw paradoxically argues that masters aren't truly free either. They are enslaved by the constant need to manage their wealth, property, and the workers. 🏢
hint: Owning a lot of things can be its own kind of trap.

question: What role do the police and the army play in an unnatural slavery system, according to Shaw? 🚔
options: They ensure the workers get fair wages 💵
They protect the property of the master class and enforce the system 🛡️
They provide food for the poor 🍲
They fight against the capitalist masters ⚔️
answer: They protect the property of the master class and enforce the system 🛡️
explanation: Fantastic! Shaw points out that the state's forces (police, army, laws) are set up to protect the property of the rich and ensure the unnatural slavery system continues. ⚖️
hint: Whose interests do they primarily defend in a capitalist society?

question: What was the original format of Shaw's essay 'Freedom'? 📻
options: A private letter to a friend ✉️
A chapter in a novel 📖
A radio broadcast for the BBC 🎙️
A speech in the parliament 🏛️
answer: A radio broadcast for the BBC 🎙️
explanation: Awesome! 'Freedom' was originally delivered as a radio broadcast. This is why the language is highly conversational, engaging, and directly addresses the listener! 🎧
hint: It was meant to be listened to, not just read.

question: What does Shaw say the rich do to ensure they have plenty of leisure time? 🏖️
options: They stop sleeping entirely 🚫
They shift their share of natural and unnatural work onto the working class 👷
They invent time machines ⏳
They do all their work very quickly ⚡
answer: They shift their share of natural and unnatural work onto the working class 👷
explanation: Brilliant! The 'idle rich' maintain their freedom by forcing the working class to do not only their own work but also the work required to maintain the rich! 🎩
hint: They make someone else do the heavy lifting.

question: What is the ultimate paradox of the 'free' citizen in a capitalist society? 🎭
options: They are completely free but choose to be slaves 🦅
They proudly call themselves free, yet spend their whole lives serving a master 🎩
They are naturally slaves but unnaturally free 🧬
They vote for masters but become masters themselves 🗳️
answer: They proudly call themselves free, yet spend their whole lives serving a master 🎩
explanation: Spot on! The great paradox is the illusion of freedom. We sing songs about liberty, yet we must beg an employer for a job just to survive. 🏢
hint: There is a massive contradiction between what they say and how they live.

question: What is 'Wage Slavery' as implied in Shaw's essay? 💵
options: Getting paid millions for doing nothing 💰
Working only for natural survival 🌿
Being legally free but economically forced to work for a master to survive 🏭
Owning slaves and paying them well 🎩
answer: Being legally free but economically forced to work for a master to survive 🏭
explanation: Excellent! You aren't in chains like a traditional slave, but you are a 'wage slave'. If you stop working, you stop getting paid, and you starve. 🍞
hint: You are chained by your paycheck rather than by iron.

question: How does Shaw characterize absolute, 100% freedom? 🕊️
options: It is easily achievable through money 💸
It is an impossible myth because of our biological needs 🧬
It exists only in the United Kingdom 🇬🇧
It is only available to politicians 🏛️
answer: It is an impossible myth because of our biological needs 🧬
explanation: Fantastic! Absolute freedom is a fantasy. Because we have physical bodies that need food and rest, we will always be slaves to nature to some degree. 🌍
hint: Can you choose not to breathe?

question: What is the difference between 'Chattel Slavery' and the slavery of the modern worker? ⛓️
options: Chattel slavery is voluntary 🙋
Modern workers are bought and sold as property 🏷️
Chattel slaves are legally owned, while modern workers are economically trapped 🏭
There is absolutely no difference 🤷
answer: Chattel slaves are legally owned, while modern workers are economically trapped 🏭
explanation: Awesome! Chattel slaves are literally owned like furniture. Modern workers are 'free' to quit, but since they must eat, they are trapped by the economy into wage slavery. 💵
hint: One involves legal ownership, the other involves financial necessity.

question: Why does Shaw believe that national anthems and patriotic songs are misleading? 🎵
options: They are too difficult to sing 🎤
They are written by the poor 🏚️
They give people a false sense of political and personal freedom 🗽
They complain too much about the government 🏛️
answer: They give people a false sense of political and personal freedom 🗽
explanation: Brilliant! Shaw mocks anthems like 'Rule Britannia' because they brainwash citizens into believing they are free, distracting them from their actual economic slavery. 🎭
hint: They make people believe something that isn't entirely true.

question: According to Shaw, what is the main commodity that a worker has to sell in a capitalist system? 🛠️
options: Their land 🏞️
Their personal time and labor ⏳
Their natural resources 💧
Their political vote 🗳️
answer: Their personal time and labor ⏳
explanation: Spot on! The only thing the working class owns is their time and physical/mental effort, which they must sell to the capitalist master to earn a living. 👷
hint: It is the effort and hours they put into a job.

question: What political ideology does Shaw's essay heavily lean towards? 🚩
options: Unregulated Capitalism 🎩
Monarchy 👑
Socialism and fair distribution of labor 🤝
Anarchy 💥
answer: Socialism and fair distribution of labor 🤝
explanation: Excellent! Shaw was a prominent socialist (a member of the Fabian Society). He believed that labor and wealth should be distributed fairly so everyone could enjoy true leisure. 🌍
hint: He advocates for fairness and against capitalist exploitation.

question: According to Shaw, how does the capitalist system disguise 'unnatural slavery'? 🎭
options: By calling it a 'vacation' 🏖️
By dressing workers in expensive clothes 👔
By calling it 'employment', 'duty', or 'honest labor' 💼
By paying workers in gold coins 🪙
answer: By calling it 'employment', 'duty', or 'honest labor' 💼
explanation: Fantastic! Society uses respectful words like 'employment' and 'hard work' to make the unnatural exploitation of humans feel noble and acceptable. 🎩
hint: They use professional-sounding words instead of 'slavery'.

question: What example does Shaw use to show that even Kings are not completely free? 👑
options: They have to pay taxes like everyone else 💸
They are bound by state duties, public appearances, and natural slavery 🏛️
They have to work in factories on weekends 🏭
They are not allowed to own property 🚫
answer: They are bound by state duties, public appearances, and natural slavery 🏛️
explanation: Awesome! A king might seem free, but he is a slave to his royal duties, his public schedule, and of course, he still has to sleep and eat like any other human! 🛌
hint: Think about the responsibilities that come with a crown.

question: If a person works an 8-hour shift, how many hours of 'true freedom' (leisure) do they actually have left, considering natural slavery? ⏳
options: 12 hours 🕛
8 hours ⌚
4 hours ⌛
0 hours 🚫
answer: 4 hours ⌛
explanation: Brilliant! Let's do the math: 24 hours in a day. Minus 12 hours for natural slavery (sleep/eat) = 12 hours left. Minus 8 hours of work = only 4 hours of true freedom! 🎸
hint: Subtract 12 (natural) and 8 (work) from 24.

question: What does Shaw imply about the 'Magna Carta' and the 'British Constitution'? 📜
options: They are flawless documents of human liberty 🕊️
They successfully ended all forms of slavery ⚖️
They are pieces of paper that fail to protect people from economic slavery 🎩
They were written by the working class 🛠️
answer: They are pieces of paper that fail to protect people from economic slavery 🎩
explanation: Spot on! Shaw argues that legal documents praising liberty are useless if the economic system still forces people into wage slavery to survive. 💸
hint: Do these old documents stop you from having to work for a boss?

question: Why is 'Nature' considered a fair master, unlike human masters? 🌿
options: Nature gives us money 💰
Nature applies its rules equally to everyone without discrimination 🌍
Nature never makes us tired ⚡
Nature lets us vote 🗳️
answer: Nature applies its rules equally to everyone without discrimination 🌍
explanation: Excellent! A capitalist master exploits the poor, but Nature makes both the billionaire and the beggar hungry and sleepy. Nature's slavery is universal and fair. 🥪
hint: It treats the rich and the poor exactly the same.

question: How does Shaw describe the conversational tone of his broadcast? 🎙️
options: Highly academic and impossible to understand 📚
Angry, aggressive, and threatening 😡
Witty, logical, simple, and direct 🗣️
Poetic and full of rhymes 🎵
answer: Witty, logical, simple, and direct 🗣️
explanation: Fantastic! Shaw deliberately used simple, engaging, and witty language because he was speaking to the general public over the radio, making complex ideas accessible. 📻
hint: Think about how you would speak to hold an audience's attention on the radio.

question: What is the primary difference between a 'master' and a 'slave' in Shaw's capitalist critique? 🎩
options: Masters are taller than slaves 📏
Masters live off the surplus labor of the slaves 💸
Masters don't have to eat or sleep 🤖
Slaves are allowed to vote, but masters are not 🗳️
answer: Masters live off the surplus labor of the slaves 💸
explanation: Awesome! The master is someone who owns the means of production and lives comfortably by taking the surplus value created by the hard work of the wage slaves. 🏭
hint: It's about who profits from the actual work being done.

question: What does Shaw mean when he mentions the 'greatest common multiple' of freedom? ➕
options: Maximizing the leisure time available for every single person in society 🏖️
Making sure the rich have all the free time 🎩
Multiplying the working hours by two ✖️
A mathematical formula for taxation 🧮
answer: Maximizing the leisure time available for every single person in society 🏖️
explanation: Brilliant! Shaw believed society should be organized so that the necessary work is shared equally, giving the 'greatest common multiple' (the maximum possible amount) of leisure to everyone. 🌍
hint: It means getting the absolute most free time for everyone.

question: What does Shaw say about Trade Unions in the context of freedom? 🛠️
options: They have successfully eliminated capitalism 🚫
They only help the master class 🎩
They try to fight wage slavery but operate within the boundaries of the capitalist system ⚖️
They force people to work longer hours ⏳
answer: They try to fight wage slavery but operate within the boundaries of the capitalist system ⚖️
explanation: Spot on! While Trade Unions try to get better wages and hours, they don't overthrow the system of unnatural slavery itself; they just try to make it slightly more bearable. 🤝
hint: They negotiate with the boss, but don't get rid of the boss.

question: According to Shaw, what illusion does formal 'education' sometimes create? 🎓
options: It makes people think they don't need to eat 🍎
It brainwashes people into accepting unnatural slavery as a normal, respectable life 📚
It makes everyone a capitalist master 🎩
It teaches people how to fly 🦅
answer: It brainwashes people into accepting unnatural slavery as a normal, respectable life 📚
explanation: Excellent! Shaw critiques an education system that trains students to be obedient workers, making them proud of their 'employment' rather than realizing they are wage slaves. 🧠
hint: It makes people accept the system without questioning it.

question: If a man refuses to engage in unnatural slavery (refuses to get a job), what is his likely fate under capitalism? ☠️
options: He is given a free house 🏠
He is praised as a hero 🦸‍♂️
He will fall victim to Nature's whip and starve 🍞
He becomes the Prime Minister 🏛️
answer: He will fall victim to Nature's whip and starve 🍞
explanation: Fantastic! You are technically 'free' to not work, but if you don't work, you don't get paid. If you don't get paid, Nature steps in and you starve to death. 🍽️
hint: Without money in a capitalist system, what happens to your body?

question: What does Shaw think about the phrase 'freedom of contract'? 📝
options: It is the best thing about capitalism 🌟
It is a joke, because a starving man has no real choice but to sign the contract 🃏
It means you can work for free 💸
It protects the workers perfectly 🛡️
answer: It is a joke, because a starving man has no real choice but to sign the contract 🃏
explanation: Awesome! A contract is only fair if both sides can walk away. A worker cannot walk away from a job contract because they will starve, making the 'freedom' an illusion. ⚖️
hint: Is it really a free choice if someone is holding a gun (or starvation) to your head?

question: Which of these activities would Shaw classify under 'Leisure' (True Freedom)? 🎨
options: Eating breakfast 🥣
Sleeping for 8 hours 🛌
Working at a factory machine ⚙️
Reading a book for pleasure 📖
answer: Reading a book for pleasure 📖
explanation: Brilliant! Eating and sleeping are natural slavery. Factory work is unnatural slavery. Reading a book just because you want to is true leisure and absolute freedom! 🕊️
hint: It must be something you do voluntarily for fun, not survival or money.

question: Why is Shaw's argument considered a 'Satire'? 🎭
options: Because it uses humor, exaggeration, and irony to criticize society's flaws 🃏
Because it is a romantic poem 🌹
Because it tells a fictional story about a wizard 🧙‍♂️
Because it is a historical timeline 📅
answer: Because it uses humor, exaggeration, and irony to criticize society's flaws 🃏
explanation: Spot on! Satire is a literary device used to mock human foolishness. Shaw uses sharp wit to expose the hypocrisy of a society that calls itself 'free' while enslaving its people. 🗣️
hint: It involves mocking or making fun of serious societal issues.

question: How does Shaw describe Nature's enforcement of its laws? 🌿
options: Gentle and forgiving 🌸
Strict, tyrannical, and inescapable ⚖️
Lazy and slow 🐢
Easily bribed with money 💸
answer: Strict, tyrannical, and inescapable ⚖️
explanation: Excellent! Nature is the ultimate tyrant. It does not care about your feelings, your wealth, or your laws; if you do not sleep and eat, you will die. ☠️
hint: Can you escape or bargain with hunger and sleep?

question: What is the primary motivation for the 'master class' to maintain the capitalist system? 🎩
options: To help the poor learn skills 📚
To ensure everyone is equal ⚖️
To secure their own leisure time and wealth by exploiting others' labor 💰
To appease Mother Nature 🌿
answer: To secure their own leisure time and wealth by exploiting others' labor 💰
explanation: Fantastic! The masters want to escape the drudgery of work. By keeping the capitalist system, they force the workers to produce the wealth that funds the masters' luxurious leisure. 🏖️
hint: They want to keep their money and free time.

question: What does Shaw imply about a society where the rich are idle and the poor are overworked? 🏚️
options: It is perfectly balanced and fair ⚖️
It is an unnatural, fundamentally unjust society 🚫
It is the only way humans can survive 🌍
It makes everyone equally happy 😄
answer: It is an unnatural, fundamentally unjust society 🚫
explanation: Awesome! Shaw deeply opposed this inequality. He believed that an unjust society allows a few to be idle while forcing the masses into lifelong unnatural slavery. 🤝
hint: He thinks it is deeply unfair and wrong.

question: What happens to the psychological state of a person trapped in lifelong unnatural slavery? 🧠
options: They become highly creative geniuses 🎨
They lose their true individuality and become a mere cog in the machine ⚙️
They achieve spiritual enlightenment ✨
They stop needing to sleep 🛌
answer: They lose their true individuality and become a mere cog in the machine ⚙️
explanation: Brilliant! Constant, repetitive labor drains a person's soul. They stop living as free, creative individuals and become just another machine part making money for the boss. 🏭
hint: They lose their humanity and become like a machine.

question: What is the crucial difference between who benefits from 'natural' vs 'unnatural' slavery? ⚖️
options: Natural slavery benefits the boss; unnatural benefits the worker 🏭
Natural slavery benefits the individual's own body; unnatural slavery benefits the capitalist master 🎩
Both benefit the government 🏛️
Neither benefits anyone 🚫
answer: Natural slavery benefits the individual's own body; unnatural slavery benefits the capitalist master 🎩
explanation: Spot on! When you eat and sleep (natural), you keep yourself alive and healthy. When you work in a factory (unnatural), the surplus value of your hard work goes into the master's pocket! 💸
hint: Think about who gets the actual reward for the effort.

question: What does Shaw's essay suggest we should do about the necessary work of society (like farming, building)? 🚜
options: Stop doing it entirely 🚫
Force only the poorest to do it 🏚️
Share the necessary labor equally so everyone gets equal leisure time 🤝
Let robots do it all immediately 🤖
answer: Share the necessary labor equally so everyone gets equal leisure time 🤝
explanation: Excellent! Shaw's socialist ideal is that if *everyone* shared the burden of necessary work, the work hours would drop dramatically, giving *everyone* plenty of leisure time! ⏳
hint: He believes in fairness and sharing the load.

question: Which word best describes the tone of the statement: 'You can choose which master to vote for, so you must be free'? 🃏
options: Sincere 💖
Sarcastic / Ironical 🎭
Scientific 🔬
Romantic 🌹
answer: Sarcastic / Ironical 🎭
explanation: Fantastic! Shaw is being highly sarcastic here. He is pointing out the absurdity of thinking you are free just because you get to choose the name of the person who will oppress you. 🗳️
hint: He is saying the opposite of what is actually true to make a point.

question: How does Shaw view the concept of 'Landlords' in his essay? 🏰
options: As generous providers of housing 🏠
As people who unfairly monopolize the Earth and force others to pay to exist on it 🌍
As the most oppressed group in society 🥺
As natural slaves 🌿
answer: As people who unfairly monopolize the Earth and force others to pay to exist on it 🌍
explanation: Awesome! Shaw attacks landlords by pointing out that the Earth belongs to everyone, yet a few people claim to 'own' it and force the rest of us to pay rent just to exist! 💸
hint: He thinks charging rent for living on the Earth is unfair.

question: Why is 'Freedom' by G.B. Shaw considered a piece of 'Non-Fiction'? 📚
options: Because it tells a magical story 🪄
Because it is entirely made up 🦄
Because it presents factual arguments, logic, and commentary on real-world society 🌍
Because it has rhyming verses 🎵
answer: Because it presents factual arguments, logic, and commentary on real-world society 🌍
explanation: Brilliant! Non-fiction deals with reality. Shaw is providing a logical, essay-style commentary on real economics, human biology, and society, not a fictional story. 🧠
hint: It is based on real life and real ideas, not imagination.

question: What illusion prevents the working class from revolting against unnatural slavery? 😵
options: They think they are already perfectly free because of democracy and national anthems 🎶
They are too busy playing video games 🎮
They are secretly all billionaires 💰
They love being whipped by the masters 💥
answer: They think they are already perfectly free because of democracy and national anthems 🎶
explanation: Spot on! The system brainwashes the working class with songs of liberty, voting rights, and legal documents, making them blind to their actual economic slavery. 🎭
hint: They have been tricked into believing a comfortable lie.

question: In Shaw's paradox, a person is technically 'free' to walk out of their job, but what makes this freedom useless? ⛓️
options: The boss will lock the door 🚪
Walking out means losing wages, which leads to starvation 🍞
It is illegal to quit a job 🚔
The worker will get lost outside 🗺️
answer: Walking out means losing wages, which leads to starvation 🍞
explanation: Excellent! You have the 'legal' freedom to quit, but not the 'economic' freedom. The invisible chain of poverty forces you to stay and submit to unnatural slavery. 💵
hint: What happens to your bank account and stomach if you quit?

question: What is Shaw's ultimate message to the listener of his broadcast? 🎙️
options: Stop eating and sleeping immediately 🚫
To critically question the false freedom sold by society and recognize our true economic conditions 🧠
To blindly obey the politicians 🏛️
To buy more land and become a master 🎩
answer: To critically question the false freedom sold by society and recognize our true economic conditions 🧠
explanation: Fantastic! Shaw's goal is to wake people up! He wants the listener to peel back the patriotic lies, recognize their economic slavery, and strive for a fairer society with true leisure. 🌅
hint: He wants you to think critically and see through the illusions.

question: Which statement best summarizes the core theme of G.B. Shaw's 'Freedom'? 🕊️
options: Humans are completely free to do whatever they want 🦅
Freedom is an absolute truth in modern democracy 🏛️
True freedom is an illusion; we are all slaves to biology, and most of us are slaves to capitalism 🌍
Only the working class is truly free 🛠️
answer: True freedom is an illusion; we are all slaves to biology, and most of us are slaves to capitalism 🌍
explanation: Awesome! This perfectly summarizes the essay. We can never escape the slavery of our bodies, but we must also realize that our 'free' society actually forces us into capitalist slavery! ⚖️
hint: It combines both the biological and economic arguments of the essay.
